units.summary: Madison, nineteen, meets apparently college-aged Amelia during summer break, begins an exclusive romance within hours, meets Amelia’s three mothers, and discovers that Amelia concealed extensive education and paramedic credentials. A cut lip prompts Amelia to taste Madison’s blood and awkwardly disguise her response. Ending state: attraction is intense, but Amelia’s first material deception and blood reaction are exposed.
units.pov: First-person retrospective Madison, tightly limited to her perceptions with occasional hindsight framing.
units.chronology: Summer break, about two weeks before summer semester. The first date and dorm dinner occur on day one; unpacking and meeting Amelia’s family occur the next day.
evidence_refs: Ch1 opening frame: vampire myths and later discovery
Ch1 park/bakery/dorm: first date and exclusivity
Ch1 Amelia’s house: June, Savannah, and Emma introduced
Ch1 bedroom: Madison’s cut lip and Amelia tasting blood
Ch1 school box: biology degree, music study, and paramedic credentials

units.summary: Nearly two weeks into dating, Amelia plays piano and Madison nearly says she loves her, establishing Madison’s fear that naming love promises loss. On the Sunday before classes, a climber falls. Amelia judges him unsalvageable, drains him, destroys and disperses the body with several spells, and removes remaining evidence. Madison follows her home while suspecting possible murder. Ending state: Amelia’s witch identity, lethal pragmatism, blood appetite, family oversight, and evidence-destruction capacity are undeniable; Madison remains physically close and morally destabilized.
units.pov: First-person Madison; sensory access is limited by shock, distance, and Amelia’s command to cover her eyes.
units.chronology: About two weeks after Ch1. The piano sequence occurs shortly before semester start; the cliff incident occurs Sunday, less than twenty-four hours before classes.
evidence_refs: Ch2 piano scene: Amelia’s melancholy and Madison’s blocked love confession
Ch2 hike: solo climber’s fatal fall
Ch2 cliff: draining, incineration, pulverizing, dispersal, terrain reversal, and rope burning
Ch2 Savannah call: lifeblood taken off schedule; family felt the work
Ch2 departure: Madison labels the event possible murder and notes slippery morals

units.summary: Amelia confirms she is a witch and technically killed the climber seconds before his natural death. She explains witch anatomy, strongholds, weak versus processed blood, intelligence-linked potency, fangs, Hunger, and activation by eating a beating heart. Madison vomits but stays. Amelia distinguishes post-activation pull from addiction and reveals that blood exposure forced her out of EMS. At Madison’s request, she performs constructive freework: shadow flowers become colored, scented, partly solid petals. Ending state: Madison accepts continued intimacy but has not resolved activation or Amelia’s killings; she gains a first structured model of magic and evidence that it can create beauty.
units.pov: First-person Madison, continuous after Ch2; emotional overload makes her an openly incomplete recorder.
units.chronology: Immediately after the climber incident, through dinner and the same night.
evidence_refs: Ch3 bedroom: witch identity and technical responsibility for the climber’s death
Ch3 anatomy lesson: fangs, two-part stronghold, remixing, weak blood, intelligence scaling
Ch3 activation disclosure: puberty Hunger and beating-heart requirement
Ch3 patio: taste, post-activation pull, addiction distinction, EMS departure
Ch3 candle/bedroom: shadow-flower freework, grimwork distinction, healing and pain limits

units.summary: On the first day of classes, Madison prioritizes gathering magical data over coursework. Amelia discloses ages and activity-linked slowed aging: Amelia is twenty-eight and very active; her mothers are roughly 140–160. Amelia detects large campus magic, describes her family’s volunteer-policing role, and takes Madison along. She demonstrates engraved tracking, invisibility, targeted shields, and rapid combat preparation. At a dorm, Mackenzie detects and dispels their concealment, trades attacks with Amelia, and invites them inside. Ending state: Madison has crossed from private revelation into an active witch community while physically participating in a risky enforcement encounter.
units.pov: First-person Madison, including timestamped text messages; she infers spell functions from incomplete observation.
units.chronology: Monday, first day of summer semester; follows directly after Ch3’s Sunday revelation.
evidence_refs: Ch4 CS205 texts: aging scales with work; family ages; Amelia is twenty-eight and very active
Ch4 lunch: local monitoring purpose and Robin’s replacement
Ch4 campus search: engraved residue compass
Ch4 dorm exterior: cutting, dripping, painting, weak human blood, and targeted shields
Ch4 hallway: large magic estimate, Mackenzie’s detection, attack/counterattack, and dispel

units.summary: Madison and Amelia meet FAWN: witches Mackenzie and Miriam and humans Olivia, Evelyn, and Zoe. FAWN stores remixed witch blood in jars while researching degradation and uses failed stock for large experiments such as growing a tree. A magically compelled truth-or-dare game exposes Amelia’s engraved compulsion spell, Madison’s willingness to be cut and heavily fed upon, Mackenzie’s violent sexuality, and Amelia’s qualified desire to make Madison a witch. Madison learns FAWN’s donations are voluntary and that it avoids lifeblood. She realizes FAWN gives her independent access to magic, then tells Amelia she loves her. Ending state: the couple remains together, but mind-control ethics and turning remain unresolved; Madison is hypovolemic, socially integrated into FAWN, and explicitly fascinated by scalable blood storage.
units.pov: First-person Madison; alcohol, blood loss, and compulsion affect reliability and judgment.
units.chronology: Continues immediately from Ch4, still Monday around lunch and into the time Madison should attend ethics class.
evidence_refs: Ch5 FAWN room: membership, blood jars, laboratory equipment, and tree
Ch5 battery discussion: degradation research and degraded blood used for growth spell
Ch5 truth-or-dare: consent discussion and engraved compulsion
Ch5 feeding: Madison accepts Mackenzie’s slash and continues past dizziness; Amelia heals her
Ch5 turning question: Amelia says yes in principle; mutual desire required
Ch5 donation explanation: rotating humans, distillation through witches, no group lifeblood
Ch5 stairwell: independent access to magic enables Madison’s love confession

units.summary: Madison tells Julia she has said she loves someone while concealing magic. She directly calls Amelia a possible serial killer. Amelia argues context and gray morality, admits one EMS feeding killed a patient, and says constant blood exposure made her leave. Madison offers future consensual feeding. Still recovering from Mackenzie, she bonds with Zoe, learns additional spell mechanics and Miriam’s lethal defensive history, and commits to weekly FAWN and human game nights. Madison then demands Amelia’s engraving count: ninety-three completed spells plus unused climber lifeblood. She immediately seeks the resource-cost model and grimoire evidence, then studies elemental symbols for hours, treating magic as a programming language. Ending state: Madison and Amelia plan to sleep together nonsexually; Madison is physically depleted but intellectually accelerating, while the human cost of Amelia’s power is now quantified.
units.pov: First-person Madison, with short scene breaks and text exchange; attraction, exhaustion, and analytic drive shape emphasis.
units.chronology: After Monday’s FAWN encounter: the Julia call and serial-killer discussion occur after the love confession; Wednesday classes, lunch, game night, and late-night mechanics lesson occupy most of the chapter.
evidence_refs: Ch6 Julia call: love disclosed without magic
Ch6 bed: serial-killer confrontation and Amelia’s gray-area defense
Ch6 EMS account: one feeding death and repeated temptation
Ch6 Zoe texts/lunch: continuing hypovolemia and attraction to Mackenzie’s evil edge
Ch6 walk: intent, sustaining, termination, and engraving-cost overview
Ch6 Zoe history: Miriam kills an assailant and refuses his lifeblood
Ch6 bedroom: 93 engravings, climber as unused 94th source, and elemental lesson

characters: Madison: nineteen, first-person narrator, exceptional programmer pursuing CS before graduate mathematics; rapidly attaches to Amelia, fears saying love because attachment predicts loss, seeks complete system knowledge, and accepts escalating bodily and ethical risk for access.

Amelia Isobel: twenty-eight, looks about twenty-one, witch with biology degree, music minor, paramedic training, ninety-three engravings, and one unused lifeblood source; powerful, very active, affectionate, apologetic, secretive, and experienced in killing and concealment.
June: Amelia’s legal mother, about 160, moderately active witch; cooks, uses checking magic, and offers gentler biological framing.
Savannah: Amelia’s legal mother, about 140, moderately active witch; monitors magic use, dislikes “muggles,” knows enforcement context, and is protective of Madison after the feeding.
Emma: straight, nearly asexual platonic life partner to June and Savannah; about 140, moderately active witch and co-parent.

Mackenzie “Mack” Jordan: witch, molecular-biology postdoc, FAWN battery lead, provocative and combative; detects concealment, uses large magic, drinks Madison close to collapse, and treats a violent sexual memory with amusement.
Miriam: calm FAWN witch who developed the tree-growth spell, drove off a dormmate, and previously killed a coercive boy by opening his throat but rejected his lifeblood.
Zoe: bubbly human FAWN member and blood donor; becomes Madison’s independent friend and secondary magic expositor.
Olivia and Evelyn: human FAWN members and rotating donors; Olivia wants to become a witch, while Evelyn proposes the drinking game.
Julia: Madison’s former girlfriend/crush and current confidante; knows only the romance layer.
Robin: previous local monitor who recently retired to Wyoming; her departure prompted Amelia’s family to move.
The climber: unnamed dying man whom Amelia drains and whose body and evidence she destroys; his lifeblood remains unused at Ch6 end.
knowledge: Madison knows Amelia, June, Savannah, Emma, Mackenzie, and Miriam are witches; Zoe, Olivia, and Evelyn are human.
Madison knows Amelia caused the climber’s death, has killed many others, has ninety-three engraved spells, and retains the climber as a potential ninety-fourth source.
Madison knows activation requires beginning to eat a beating heart and distinguishes pre-activation Hunger from post-activation pull and possible addiction.
Madison knows stronghold and fang anatomy at overview level, but not full biology, reproductive mechanics, pregnancy conditions, or turning consequences.

Madison knows weak blood, remixed strong blood, lifeblood-linked engraving, intent, symbol interruption, depletion, and some size/potency relationships; her understanding is partly secondhand and untested.

Madison knows Amelia left EMS because of blood temptation and that one EMS feeding killed someone, but lacks the circumstances, victim context, accountability, and whether this death funded an engraving.
Madison knows FAWN’s battery stock comes from voluntary rotating human donors, is processed through witches, degrades, and can power large work; she does not know preservation theory or firm limits.
Madison knows Amelia’s family replaced Robin in local monitoring, but not the authority structure, enforcement record, Portland history, or Amelia’s past actions as a monitor.
Amelia knows Madison is fascinated, wants exhaustive information, accepts cutting and feeding risks, loves her, and is relieved to have magic access independent of their relationship.
FAWN knows Madison is newly informed, human, Amelia’s partner, unusually bold, and willing to donate; it has no evidence yet of Madison’s proposed spell-design aptitude.
Julia knows Madison rapidly fell in love and made new friends, but not that witches or magic exist.
relationships: Madison–Amelia: rapid exclusive romance becomes mutual declared love; attraction and tenderness coexist with deception, lethal moral conflict, access dependency, protectiveness, and unresolved compulsion and turning questions.
Madison–magic: progresses from worldview rupture and nausea to structured fascination, risk-taking, independent social access, and sustained technical study.
Madison–FAWN: moves from intruder to welcomed prospective regular; the group supplies community and knowledge independent of Amelia, but Mackenzie has already violated safe feeding boundaries.
Amelia–FAWN: wary cooperation after an enforcement-style confrontation; Mackenzie frames Amelia as authoritarian or “Gestapo,” while Amelia suspects reckless or indiscriminate lifeblood use.
Amelia–mothers: close, protective, and operationally coordinated; they detect her large work and expect reporting, but their exact authority over her is unclear.
Madison–Zoe: fast-forming friendship grounded in FAWN membership, shared human status, game night, and exposition; Zoe normalizes dangerous witch behavior.
Mackenzie–FAWN: Mackenzie provokes and leads research; Miriam moderates but accepts risky compulsion play; the humans trust them despite known aggression.
Miriam–Zoe: high-school friendship survived Zoe witnessing Miriam kill an assailant.
Madison–Katherine: only indirectly evidenced as a weird home relationship and Madison’s avoidance; the extensive Henot and grimoire conflict in notes has not entered the manuscript.
Madison–Julia: former romantic failure turned friendship; Julia is a safe recipient for partial truths.
physical_state: Madison’s Ch1 lip cut stops bleeding normally; no lasting injury is recorded.
The climber is drained, incinerated, pulverized, dispersed, and his scene altered; rope evidence is burned. No body remains.
Amelia cuts her forearms repeatedly; rapid healing leaves visible fresh lines and faint older scars. Pain is reduced, not eliminated, and witch skin is described as fragile.
Madison’s palm is cut for invisibility in Ch4; the later state of that wound is not explicitly tracked.

Mackenzie slashes Madison’s arm and drinks until Madison cannot stand and her vision darkens; Amelia magically closes the wound, but hypovolemia, exhaustion, breathlessness, and impaired walking persist through Ch6.

Amelia is depleted after shielding and healing at FAWN but retains the climber’s lifeblood because she refuses to spend it; by late Ch6 she has replenished enough for demonstrations, source unspecified.
FAWN’s room contains jars of remixed blood at varying degradation states, lab equipment, chemicals, failed samples, butcher paper, and a magically grown potted tree.
Amelia carries a purse with phone, cleanup cloth, and bag; she owns a locked chest and a grimoire that is not present at Madison’s dorm in Ch6.
Amelia creates a warm, rough, translucent purple heart gem synchronized to her heartbeat and gives it to Madison; its location after the garden scene is unstated.
Amelia’s house, garden bench, piano room, bedroom, Madison’s dorm, FAWN’s converted dorm room, campus classrooms, Zoe’s dorm, and the cliff are established locations.
world_rules: Witches are treated as a human-compatible subspecies with retractable hollow finger fangs and a two-part stronghold that digests blood and stores distilled magic for remixing into their own blood.
Magic is active in or created alongside blood; potency scales sharply with intelligence. Human blood is strong relative to animals; unprocessed blood is called weak.

Activation usually occurs around puberty after escalating Hunger and requires beginning to consume a beating heart. Afterward, immediate blood produces a controllable pull; addiction is distinct but facilitated by exposure.
Witches heal and replenish blood faster, can reduce but not erase pain, may have fragile skin, and age more slowly in proportion to magical work.
Magic is executed through blood-drawn symbols plus witch intent. Cutting can use subject blood; dripping or painting can use prepared blood; humans lack activation intent.
Engraving compresses a larger spell into a personal symbol and consumes all stored magic from one lifeblood source regardless of final symbol size; the manuscript does not yet fully explain aliasing.
Freework is improvised full-symbol casting; grimwork is preplanned or grimoire-based full-symbol casting; engraved work is faster and more blood-efficient.
Spell scale depends on symbol or blood amount and blood type, with spell-specific minimums. Intent can target, sustain with remixed blood, or stop work; depletion or a broken symbol can terminate it.
Large work can be sensed at a distance and leaves residue that an engraved compass can follow. Concealment and shields can be detected or dispelled by suitable magic.

Blood batteries store remixed witch blood for later use, but potency degrades. FAWN establishes that blood prepared by one witch can apparently support group work; the precise activation or claim rule is deferred.

Witches can magically compel truth and action. Amelia’s spell requires continuing intent shifts and cannot simply be toggled for each turn; consent is a social safeguard, not a demonstrated mechanical requirement.
Slowed aging, local monitoring, and sensing imply accumulated power and enforcement pressures, but jurisdiction, penalties, secrecy law, and population are not established in chapters 1–6.
The manuscript has not established fungal-spore theory, recursion or Turing limits, stamps, conception rules, sex-linked inheritance, stronghold-violation taboo, or exact turning mechanics.

arcs: Madison’s revelation arc: romance-driven normalcy → lethal magical discovery → biological horror → constructive wonder → social entry → technical apprenticeship.

Madison’s dark-aptitude arc: she labels her morals slippery, analyzes death before fully grieving it, chooses physical risk, remains fascinated by batteries, values independent magical access, quantifies Amelia’s kills, and treats symbols as code. This is legible setup, not yet an enacted atrocity or independent spell.

Amelia’s moral-exposure arc: charming young newcomer → secretive trained adult → pragmatic killer and evidence destroyer → traumatized witch seeking acceptance → local enforcer → admitted repeat killer with an EMS death and ninety-three engravings.

Romance arc: immediate attraction and exclusivity → concealment fracture → intimacy survives horror → FAWN removes access dependency → Madison declares love → Amelia reciprocates with the heart gem. Trust remains conditional and ethically unstable.
Magic-learning arc: visual spectacle and anatomy overview → operational tracking and defense → batteries and compulsion → intent, termination, and lifeblood clarification → elemental-symbol lesson.
FAWN integration arc: threatening unknown magic source → tense confrontation → communal initiation → invitation and numbers exchanged → Madison commits to weekly participation.

Family/home arc: Madison avoids a weird home and struggles to name love; Amelia’s three-mother household offers warmth and oversight. Katherine-specific conflict is deferred beyond the supplied chapters.
subplots: Amelia’s EMS past: credentials in Ch1, addiction disclosure in Ch3, and one fatal feeding in Ch6; causality and accountability remain incomplete.
Amelia’s piano and melancholy: music reveals brooding complexity and gives Madison language for controlled power; it has emotional payoff but no plot payoff yet.
Local witch policing: Robin’s retirement prompted Amelia’s move; FAWN perceives Amelia’s approach as authoritarian. Formal rules and Amelia’s history remain missing.
FAWN battery research: degradation, voluntary source cycle, remixing, and large-spell use are established; preservation method and fungal theory are deferred.
Turning a human into a witch: introduced through compelled truth, then partly reassured as mutual and intimate; Amelia repeatedly defers mechanics.
Madison’s education: CS is pragmatic and programming is her strongest practiced skill; mathematics is her preferred intellectual future. Magic competes with school and maps onto code.
Madison’s human friendships: Julia receives partial romantic truth; Zoe and game night provide non-romantic support and normalize FAWN.
Blood appetite and consent: Amelia’s pull, Mackenzie’s excessive feeding, voluntary donations, possible couple feeding, and magical compulsion test bodily autonomy.
Katherine, Frieda Henot, grimoire, and tracker: prominent in notes but absent from manuscript evidence through Ch6; this is planned future material, not a current on-page subplot.
promises: Opening promise: vampire mythology has a supernatural seed but literal vampires do not; witches will explain the myth.
The climber’s unused lifeblood promises a consequential choice about Amelia’s ninety-fourth engraving and its purpose.
Amelia’s ninety-three-spell grimoire promises an evidentiary tour of past killings, spell functions, and the utility bought by each death.
Amelia’s EMS fatality and blood addiction promise a fuller, less sanitized account; current evidence gives outcome but not incident detail.
The turning conversation promises exact reproductive mechanics, costs, activation consequences, and a real choice for Madison; it is repeatedly deferred in Ch5–6.
Madison’s independent relationship with FAWN promises participation in battery research and access to magic that does not depend on Amelia.
Battery degradation and storage promise experimentation, scaling pressure, and ethical conflict; Madison’s fascination is explicit.
Amelia’s family moving to monitor local witches promises enforcement conflicts, especially with anti-authoritarian Mackenzie.
The heart gem promises continued symbolic or functional significance as reassurance and a model for heart-linked magic, though no further use occurs within coverage.
Madison’s immediate CS analogies promise original spell design and optimization; chapters 1–6 end before she casts or designs independently.
Madison’s fear of saying love receives a partial payoff when she tells Amelia, but the underlying parents and home explanation remains deferred.
Large, detectable magic and counter-detection promise escalation beyond private lessons; no tracker or antagonist is evidenced yet.
Intentional deferrals supported on-page: detailed turning mechanics, grimoire review, full culture and history lesson, EMS detail, and the function of many engravings.

Missing rather than clearly deferred evidence: exact dates and year, formal secrecy consequences, complete lifeblood acquisition history, robust battery-control rules, and safeguards or aftercare for feeding and compulsion.
motifs: Blood as appetite, fuel, evidence, intimacy, injury, research material, and moral price.
Programming and mathematical language: chapter titles, branches, compiling and DLL analogies, control language, data gathering, and optimization-minded questioning.
Hands and fingers: handholding anchors romance; fangs, cuts, symbols, feeding, and intent turn hands into instruments of intimacy and violence.
Eyes and visibility: staring begins the romance; pupils dilate around blood; candle shadows resemble an eye; invisibility, detection, and watching structure magical conflict.
Hunger and consumption: pastries, dinners, Amelia’s starvation language, activation, blood taste, feeding, and Madison’s post-loss need for food overlap desire with danger.
Light, dark, and shadow: white destruction, colored shadow flowers, invisibility, red and black combat manifestations, and elemental affinities mirror moral ambiguity.
Music and controlled power: nocturnes frame Amelia as brooding, restrained, and potentially powerful.
Names and labels: witch, muggle, vampire, serial killer, turning, Gestapo, goodie, and FAWN contest who controls moral framing.
Home, rooms, and thresholds: dorms, Amelia’s family house, locked or closed rooms, and doors mark entry into deeper knowledge and communities.
Laughter as masking and regulation: Amelia’s frequent giggling softens fear and shame; Mackenzie laughs through violence; group laughter releases tension.
Breath and heart rhythms: climber death, activation, hypovolemia, Madison’s panic, and the synchronized heart gem connect life to power and attachment.

Notes’ Katherine, Frieda, grimoire, and tracker arc has no on-page setup beyond Madison’s weird home avoidance and Amelia’s absent grimoire; treating it as active payoff would exceed evidence.
conflicts: Tone conflict: notes seek grim-dark and a sharper, less apologetic Amelia; the manuscript frequently presents her as cheerful, giggling, blushing, guilty, and reassurance-seeking. Killing, concealment, compulsion engraving, and the EMS death provide darkness, but narration often cushions them.

Amelia characterization conflict: notes want weary acceptance, volatility, possessiveness, and grim satisfaction; on-page she repeatedly apologizes, defends herself gently, accepts Madison’s framing, and shows little explicit thrill in lifeblood or power.

Serial-killer framing conflict: notes propose less defensive resignation or anger; Ch6 has Amelia cite superheroes and technical definitions, seek moral credit, and touch Madison hesitantly—more defensive and apologetic than intended.

EMS emphasis conflict: notes call for a raw, darker account; Ch6 reveals one feeding death but summarizes it briefly, hedges frequency, and omits victim, choice, consequence, and Amelia’s emotional response.

Madison dark-arc alignment: her programming-shaped fascination, need for access, quantified thinking, battery interest, and moral slippage are clear. She still reacts strongly to activation and killing; this is credible early tension, not yet full descent.

Blood-magic comprehensibility strength: chapters establish anatomy, blood classes, intent, spell forms, engraving, scale, sensing, and termination across repeated scenes. Exposition is heavy and dispersed among Amelia and Zoe, with some rules introduced only after prior use.

Blood-source terminology gap: the manuscript says engraving consumes a person’s stored lifeblood and Amelia counts ninety-three sources, but does not fully distinguish killing, last-moment draining, and sources obtained without murder; Madison equates the count with kills while Amelia does not clearly correct her.
Activation biology mostly matches notes, but lasting trauma is shown chiefly through tears and nausea; post-activation psychological consequences beyond addiction remain underdeveloped.
Stronghold explanation mostly matches notes, but the heart connection and whether magic is created by blood or merely alongside it remain explicitly uncertain.

Battery-rule gap: FAWN shows multi-user stored blood and explains preparation, but the manuscript does not state who can claim or activate a jar, whether first intent controls it, or how preservation changes safe use.

Power-accounting ambiguity: Amelia tells FAWN she is empty after healing Madison but later admits she retained climber lifeblood and merely refused to use it. This can be intentional compartmentalization, but the distinction between ordinary reserves and reserved lifeblood is not explicit.

Healing and feeding continuity: Madison’s severe symptoms persist for days, consistent with witch healing not applying to humans, but no medical monitoring or firm recovery boundary follows near-syncope, weakening consent and aftercare realism.

Consent conflict: Amelia insists on consent before compulsion, yet owns an engraved dare-enforcement spell and cannot toggle it per participant. The text notices this tension but does not explain why she engraved it or what safeguards exist.

Turning conflict with notes: the manuscript confirms mutual desire and intimacy but withholds sex, blood, orgasm, intent, pregnancy, Hunger, and activation mechanics. Notes are unresolved on pregnancy certainty, so neither version is settled canon.

Witch reproduction gap: Ch3 says witches have their own reproductive method and June calls it beautiful; chapters 1–6 do not establish female-only witches, witch-witch inheritance, human-offspring rules, or surname patterns.

Society and population gap: the manuscript establishes local volunteer monitoring and Portland’s authoritarian reputation only through partisan dialogue. Notes’ population estimates, university clustering, lineage names, and broader organization are absent.
Mechanical ontology tension: Ch3 says magic is only active in and created by blood, then allows it may be created alongside blood; notes preserve this uncertainty. Treat the ontology as unresolved.

Spell-size nuance: Ch4 uses larger weak-blood symbols for sufficient power; Ch6 says engraving size does not affect lifeblood cost and light-circle size determines duration. These can coexist, but casting size, effect parameters, and engraving cost need clearer separation.
Amelia’s age deception is acknowledged, but Ch1’s gap-year presentation plus Ch4’s reference to lying more than once leaves the precise sequence of repeated lies under-specified.

Notes place Madison’s heart-tattoo spell and game-night mechanics among recent developments, but chapters 1–6 contain only Amelia’s heart gem and Zoe’s explanation; Madison has not performed a spell. Those notes are prospective, not manuscript accomplishments.

Notes say Katherine’s arrival and Henot lineage are developing; no Katherine, Frieda, Henot surname, grimoire retrieval, tracker, attack, or bodyguard evidence occurs in the supplied chapters. This is future planning, not present manuscript fact.

Author notes say no fathers are involved in witch conception while also saying witch-human male conception produces human children; the wording is internally ambiguous and cannot be harmonized from manuscript evidence.
Author notes leave recursion, Turing completeness, and turning certainty undecided. Chapters 1–6 supply no resolving evidence.

Evidence-reliability cautions: Savannah is misspelled “Savanna” in Ch4 texts; several tense and typo slips occur; Ch2’s Chopin catalog descriptions are internally unreliable. These do not alter the main plot facts but caution against over-literal harmonization.

omissions: No manuscript material beyond Chapter 6 was treated as evidence, even where notes quote or summarize Chapter 7.
Scene boundaries are inferred from breaks, temporal transitions, and location changes because scenes are not numbered.
No long manuscript passages are reproduced; evidence references are paraphrased.
Exact dates, year, campus or town name, and several character ages are not supplied.
Note-only plans are distinguished from on-page facts, and author-note TBDs remain unresolved.
Full spell inventories and minor details are omitted unless they bear chronology, motifs, relationships, physical state, or mechanics.
